title: Address Spaces, Storage Abstraction, Virtualization & OS Functions

paras: A cumulative chapter connecting CPU memory addressing to Linux block devices, virtual storage pools, containers, virtual machines and OS scheduling.

CPU addresses identify locations in a process or physical address domain. Storage devices expose blocks, which file systems can organize as files; object storage exposes a different API. Virtualization creates logical views of compute and storage resources. The operating system manages processes, memory, files, devices, access control and scheduling. Each layer has its own identifiers, permissions and failure modes.

For a byte-addressable address domain with n bits, there are 2 n distinct addresses . Thus 32 bits give 2 32 bytes = 4 GiB ; 64 bits give 2 64 bytes = 16 EiB as a mathematical upper bound, not a promise of installed or supported RAM. Modern CPUs may implement fewer virtual and physical address bits. Process virtual address space is distinct from physical RAM, and the MMU/page tables translate addresses.

A physical address identifies a location in the machine's physical address map, which can include RAM and memory-mapped I/O. It does not necessarily identify a one-byte hardware cell or a literal external CPU pin. Page frames are fixed-size units of physical memory used by paging; common 4 KiB pages are one example.

blocks.h2: Block, file and object storage are interfaces
paras: Block: addressable sectors or logical blocks exposed by a device, SAN LUN, virtual disk or cloud block volume. File: named files and directories with permissions and metadata, provided by a file system and potentially exported via NFS/SMB. Object: objects addressed through an API and key/bucket-style namespace, commonly HTTP-based (for example S3-compatible APIs). A file system is often built on block storage, but object storage is not simply another level above file storage in every implementation.

Storage virtualization presents logical storage independently of the precise underlying disks or devices. Examples include Linux LVM logical volumes, RAID, SAN virtualization, thin provisioning and distributed storage. Some solutions aggregate many devices; others virtualize a single device, or map remote resources. /dev/sda and /dev/sdb are Linux block-device names, not proof that a device is a physical HDD; names and enumeration may change. NVMe devices commonly use names such as /dev/nvme0n1 .

Physical disks / remote volumes → RAID / LVM / storage pool → logical block volume → filesystem → mount point Do not equate storage virtualization with memory virtualization: they solve different resource-abstraction problems.

Linux containers run isolated user-space processes while sharing the host Linux kernel . Namespaces provide views of resources (PID, mount, network, user and others); cgroups account for and constrain resources; capabilities, seccomp and LSM policies can reduce privileges. Image layers and overlay filesystems commonly provide a writable container filesystem view, but not every container runtime requires OverlayFS. Containers are not complete guest operating systems.

Host Linux kernel ├── Container A: processes + libraries + mount/network namespaces └── Container B: processes + libraries + mount/network namespaces Docker and Podman are container tools; Kubernetes orchestrates workloads and is not itself a kernel virtualization mechanism. OpenVZ is a different OS-level virtualization technology.

A hypervisor virtualizes hardware resources so each VM can boot a guest OS and its own kernel . KVM is a Linux kernel virtualization facility commonly used with QEMU; VMware and Oracle VirtualBox are additional examples of virtualization stacks. Guest virtual disks may be image files ( .qcow2 , .vmdk , .vdi ), block volumes or passthrough devices; the extension depends on the platform, not on the definition of a VM.

Physical server → hypervisor → VM A (guest kernel + apps) → VM B (guest kernel + apps) VM isolation is generally stronger at the kernel boundary than ordinary shared-kernel containers, but actual security depends on configuration and vulnerabilities.

Core OS functions include process/thread creation and scheduling; virtual memory and physical memory allocation; filesystem and storage management; device-driver and I/O coordination; identities, permissions and isolation; networking; interfaces such as system calls and shells; and accounting, logs and diagnostics. The CPU executes instructions ; the kernel sets policy and manages resources . CPU scheduling involves scheduler policies, run queues and dispatch/context switching, not an administrator literally handing each process a processor.
In Linux, tools such as ps , top , free , lsblk , mount , ip and journalctl let you inspect distinct layers. Performance monitoring and job scheduling may also involve separate user-space services.

All six originals are unchanged. The explanations distinguish mathematical address width from implemented hardware limits; physical from virtual addresses; block/file/object APIs from virtualization; containers from full VMs; and CPU execution from OS scheduling. This is not a verbatim transcription or a complete hardware-specific specification.

Editorial policy: never silently replace a handwritten claim. For each correction record the original idea, precise misconception, mechanism, realistic scenario, verification path and cross-links. These explanations are curated examples across existing chapters; they do not certify that every historical statement has been reviewed.
Original idea / misconception: Artifactory is only a local disk for packages.

Correct mechanism: JFrog Artifactory is a repository manager: its metadata and artifact binaries have distinct persistence concerns. Depending on edition, configuration and supported providers, binary storage may use local filesystems or remote object storage such as S3-compatible or cloud object stores. Its HTTP repository endpoints are not the same as its physical storage location. A binary provider configuration, permissions, replication, cache and backup strategy determine actual placement and durability.

Practical example: A CI pipeline publishes a 1.2 GB application image to an internal Artifactory Docker repository. Developers pull from https://artifacts.example.com, while the administrator configures supported cloud object storage as the binary backend. Developers do not need direct object-store credentials; Artifactory authenticates requests, resolves metadata and serves the artifacts.
Verification / implementation: Check the deployment’s supported binary-provider configuration and storage diagnostics; do not infer backend location from the repository URL.

Original idea / misconception: OCI registries are specifically for microservices.

Correct mechanism: An OCI registry implements distribution APIs for content-addressed manifests and blobs. Container images are common, but OCI artifacts can represent images for a monolithic service, batch jobs, tools, Helm charts or other supported artifact types. OCI packaging says how artifacts are described and transported, not whether the application uses microservices. Support for arbitrary OCI artifacts depends on registry and client.

Practical example: A single large Java monolith is packaged as one OCI image and deployed as one Kubernetes Deployment. The same registry also holds a small command-line utility image and a Helm chart artifact. None of these is required to be a microservice.
Verification / implementation: Inspect image manifests and media types with a compatible OCI client; distinguish image identity (digest) from mutable tags.
Related source chapter: C26
Original idea / misconception: A container automatically uses its host’s IP address.

Correct mechanism: A container normally has a network namespace, whose interfaces, routes and addresses depend on the runtime’s network mode. Docker bridge networking typically gives the container its own private address; outbound traffic may be NATed through the host and inbound access may require published ports. Host-network mode shares the host network namespace, but it is an explicit choice. Kubernetes normally gives each Pod its own routable Pod IP shared by containers in that Pod; a Service exposes a stable virtual address and Ingress/Gateway routes external HTTP traffic. Exact behavior depends on the CNI, node and cluster networking design.

Practical example: A Docker web app listens on port 8080 inside a bridge-networked container. Publishing -p 8080:8080 makes it reachable through the host address, but the container’s own IP remains different. In Kubernetes, two containers in the same Pod can communicate over localhost, while a different Pod uses the Pod IP or a Service name.

Verification / implementation: Try docker inspect and docker network inspect; compare docker run --network bridge with --network host in a safe lab. In Kubernetes inspect kubectl get pods -o wide and kubectl get svc.
Related source chapter: C26
Original idea / misconception: A virtual repository stores another physical copy of every artifact.

Correct mechanism: An Artifactory virtual repository is a logical aggregation endpoint over selected local and remote repositories. It provides one resolution path and can apply routing and security rules; it does not necessarily materialize a full duplicate of all artifacts. Remote repositories may cache fetched content under their configured cache policies, and local repositories hold published binaries. Repository layout, access controls and cache behavior must be considered separately.

Practical example: A Maven build uses one virtual URL that aggregates company-release, company-snapshot and a remote Maven Central proxy. The developer configures a single endpoint. Some external dependencies are fetched and cached when first requested; the virtual repository itself is not a new physical mirror of everything.
Verification / implementation: Review virtual repository membership, remote caching settings and storage usage rather than counting repository URLs as independent copies.
Related source chapter: C26
Original idea / misconception: UART and USART are identical, and all device communication buses behave similarly.

Correct mechanism: UART denotes asynchronous serial transmit/receive logic, commonly using TX/RX plus a shared ground and agreed baud rate. USART hardware supports synchronous as well as asynchronous modes where implemented. I²C is a shared, addressed, typically two-signal board-level bus (SDA/SCL) with pull-ups; SPI is a clocked, typically short-range peripheral interface using clock, data and chip-select lines, often with separate MOSI/MISO. CAN is a differential multi-node bus designed for robust arbitration and fault handling in electrically noisy environments. Electrical levels, transceivers, framing and software drivers matter: a UART peripheral is not automatically RS-232 compatible.

Practical example: A microcontroller reads a temperature sensor over I²C, streams debugging logs through a UART-to-USB adapter, communicates with fast flash storage using SPI, and exchanges engine-control messages over CAN through a CAN transceiver. These interfaces serve different physical and protocol needs.
Verification / implementation: Check the board schematic, controller datasheet, voltage levels, termination/pull-ups, clocking and driver configuration before wiring.
Related source chapter: C26
Original idea / misconception: MQTT is another wireless radio alongside Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.

Correct mechanism: MQTT is an application-layer publish/subscribe messaging protocol, commonly carried over TCP/IP and often protected with TLS. Clients publish to topics through a broker; subscribers receive matching messages. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth are connectivity technologies with their own radio/link stacks. MQTT may run over Wi-Fi, Ethernet, cellular or other compatible IP connectivity; it does not define a radio modulation scheme. Delivery semantics such as QoS 0/1/2 are application protocol behavior, not a guarantee that a physical wireless link never fails.

Practical example: A greenhouse sensor connects to a Wi-Fi access point, obtains an IP address, establishes a TLS connection to an MQTT broker and publishes greenhouse/temperature. A dashboard on wired Ethernet subscribes to that topic. Wi-Fi moves packets; MQTT organizes messages.
Verification / implementation: Use a packet capture or broker client to inspect MQTT CONNECT/PUBLISH/SUBSCRIBE; separately inspect Wi-Fi association and IP connectivity.
Related source chapter: C26
Original idea / misconception: A 64-bit processor necessarily exposes 2^64 bytes of RAM.

Correct mechanism: Virtual address width, physical address width, implemented page-table modes and installed memory are distinct. A byte-addressed n-bit address space has up to 2^n addressable byte positions, but a CPU may implement fewer than 64 virtual and physical address bits. OS mappings, reserved regions and memory-management features constrain usable ranges. Physical RAM capacity depends on the platform, motherboard and memory modules.

Practical example: A 64-bit Linux server may have 32 GiB of installed RAM while supporting much larger virtual address spaces per process. Two processes can each map the same virtual address to different physical pages.
Verification / implementation: On Linux compare lscpu address sizes, free -h, /proc/meminfo and /proc/<pid>/maps; these measure different things.
Related source chapter: C27
Original idea / misconception: Block-level storage itself necessarily combines disks and organizes files.

Correct mechanism: Block storage exposes logical block devices and reads/writes addressed blocks. A filesystem layered above a block device manages directories, filenames, permissions and file metadata. Object storage exposes objects and metadata through an API, often accessed by bucket/key. Storage virtualization (LVM, RAID, SAN virtualization, software-defined storage) may aggregate, remap or provision storage, but aggregation is not a prerequisite for block access.

Practical example: An EC2-style VM attaches a block volume, formats it ext4 and mounts /data. A NAS exports a filesystem over NFS. An object bucket stores backups via S3 APIs. LVM may span multiple underlying disks, but ext4 is still responsible for the directory tree.
Verification / implementation: Compare lsblk, findmnt, lvs, df -h and an object-store client; they show different abstraction layers.
Related source chapter: C27
Original idea / misconception: Each container has its own independent operating-system kernel, or is as isolated as a VM.

Correct mechanism: A conventional VM virtualizes hardware and runs its own guest kernel; a conventional Linux container shares the host Linux kernel while isolating selected resources using namespaces, cgroups, capabilities and other security mechanisms. A container image can include user-space files and libraries without containing a running independent kernel. Containers may be nested inside VMs; stronger sandbox runtimes may use microVMs or separate kernels. Neither model is automatically secure without configuration.

Practical example: A physical host runs two KVM guests: one Linux and one Windows, each with its own kernel. Inside the Linux guest, three Docker containers run separate applications using that guest’s Linux kernel.
Verification / implementation: Compare uname -r in containers on one host, inspect namespace links in /proc, and compare guest kernel versions across VMs.
Related source chapter: C27
Original idea / misconception: Memory allocation and process scheduling are both done directly by the CPU.

Correct mechanism: The OS kernel manages virtual memory, page mappings, protection and allocation policies with hardware MMU support. CPU hardware executes instructions and translates memory accesses using the MMU/TLB. The kernel scheduler decides which runnable thread executes on a CPU; dispatch and context switching enact those decisions. Drivers, interrupt handlers and device controllers participate in I/O.

Practical example: When two applications compete for CPU, Linux scheduling policies determine runnable-thread execution. When an application calls mmap, the kernel establishes a mapping; physical pages may be populated lazily on page faults.
Verification / implementation: Inspect top/ps, /proc/<pid>/maps, vmstat and perf in an authorized lab; separate scheduler decisions from hardware execution.
Related source chapter: C27

   └── Container B: processes + libraries + mount/network namespaces
